# Titanic hypotheses generated by a GFlowNet

Question: is a GFlowNet a sensible engine for "universal analytics", i.e. for generating
the hypotheses of a Kaggle solution (which feature to derive from which column, which
model settings) instead of a human writing them? This branch answers it on Titanic with a
controlled comparison against random search and Optuna TPE at the same evaluation budget.

The GFlowNet infrastructure is the one from `gfn/` (U-Net policy, trajectory balance,
uniform backward policy). Only the environment, the operation library and the reward are
new. No hypothesis is hand-written: the policy decides which cells to paint.

## The molecule analogy

A full training pipeline is the object being generated, like a molecule: atoms are
(column, operation) cells and hyper-parameter values; the canvas is assembled one cell at
a time in any order (a DAG, not a tree); the reward is a cheap pre-clinical trial (seeded
5-fold CV); a Kaggle submission is the actual trial and is far too expensive and rate
limited to be the reward.

## Canvas

Rows are the 10 raw columns, columns are 8 operations. A cell may only be painted when the
operation applies to the column's type (30 valid cells out of 80); four extra rows hold
discretised hyper-parameters with at most one painted cell per row.

| column type | columns | operations allowed |
|---|---|---|
| numeric | Pclass, Age, SibSp, Parch, Fare | `raw`, `qbin` (4 quantile bins fitted on the train fold), `count` |
| numeric with missing values | Age, Fare | additionally `log` (log1p) and `missing` (indicator) |
| binary category | Sex | `raw` as 0/1 |
| low-cardinality category | Pclass, Embarked | `onehot` with a fixed category list; `missing` for Embarked |
| high-cardinality / id-like | Ticket | `count` (frequency among fit rows plus the row itself), `extract` (alphabetic prefix present) |
| structured string | Name, Cabin | `extract` (title from Name, deck letter from Cabin); `missing` for Cabin |
| counter pair | SibSp, Parch | `family` (FamilySize, IsAlone) |

Hyper-parameter rows: model ∈ {logreg, hgb}, depth ∈ {2, 3, 4}, learning rate ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2},
iterations ∈ {50, 100, 200}; an unpainted row means the default (hgb, 3, 0.1, 100).

Every fitted statistic (bin edges, counts, medians) comes from the training fold only.

## Reward

`log R = β · (cv_accuracy − 0.78)` with β = 60, cv_accuracy from a seeded stratified 5-fold
CV of the pipeline. Accuracy itself would give an almost flat distribution (0.78 vs 0.84 is
an 8 % difference); with β = 60 a 0.84 pipeline is sampled e^3.6 ≈ 37 times more often
than a 0.78 one, while CV noise (≈ 0.015) costs a factor of ≈ 2.5. Each unique hypothesis is
evaluated once (exact cache keyed by the cell set and hyper-parameters); a batch's new
hypotheses are evaluated in a 3-process pool. Everything is seeded; the trajectory sampler
uses its own `torch.Generator`.

## Controls

`compare.py` runs random search (each valid cell on with probability 1/2, hyper-parameters
uniform) and Optuna TPE (30 booleans + 4 categoricals, seeded) with the same evaluator and
the same number of unique evaluations the GFlowNet used, and reports best accuracy, the
number of distinct hypotheses above 0.83 / 0.84 and the mean of the top 20.

## Run

```bash
python -m titanic_gfn.train --iters 300 --batch 32 --workers 3     # ~15 min on 4 cores
python -m titanic_gfn.compare                                       # random + TPE at the same budget
```
